Stage 3 · Grammar

The activity, or the result?

Both tenses reach up to now. They point at different things.

Read these four sentences from the programme.
  • Climate change has been causing higher temperatures.
  • Governments have been trying to reduce pollution.
  • We haven’t been very successful so far.
  • One team of scientists has discovered a way to use lasers.
Why is the last sentence simple and not continuous?
One form reports what has been achieved. The other reports what somebody has been busy with.

Both of these forms connect the past to the present, and both are perfect forms. The difference lies in the angle from which the speaker looks at the stretch of time. The simple looks at it from outside, as a completed whole, and draws attention to the result. The continuous looks at it from inside and draws attention to the activity and how long it has been going on.

Take a piece of research. Scientists have explored several techniques reports an achievement: this is what they now have. Scientists have been exploring several techniques reports an occupation: this is what they have been doing, and it may not have produced anything yet. Both sentences can be true of the same project; they answer different questions.

Two question words map onto the two forms almost perfectly and are the fastest practical guide. How long asks about duration and pulls the continuous. How many or how much asks about a completed quantity and pulls the simple. How long have you been reading it? versus How many pages have you read? Trying to count with the continuous — I’ve been writing three emails — is one of the clearest signals that the distinction has not been grasped.

The continuous also has a use that has nothing to do with duration: explaining something visible right now, even if the activity has just stopped. You’re out of breath — have you been running? And one restriction cuts across everything: state verbs have no continuous form at all, so with know, own, believe, belong the simple is your only option even when you mean duration.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows the two forms side by side with the question each one answers. The word been is the visible marker of the continuous — look for it in every example.
The two tenses, side by side
 Simple — have/has + participleContinuous — have/has been + -ing
Points atthe result — what is finished, or how manythe activity — how long it has been going on

With numbersyes — I’ve read three reports.no — not I’ve been reading three reports.
Typical companyalready, just, yet, ever, three times, twicefor, since, all morning, lately, recently, How long…?
ExampleThey have discovered a solution.They have been working on it for years.
The same situation, two ways of seeing it
SentenceWhat it says
I’ve painted the kitchen.The job is done. Come and look.
I’ve been painting the kitchen.That is why I am covered in paint. It may not be finished.
She’s written three reports.Three finished reports exist.
She’s been writing reports all week.That is what she has been busy with.

Ask what you want the listener to notice. The finished thing, or the time spent on it? We’ve reduced pollution announces a result; we’ve been trying to reduce pollution describes the effort, and quietly admits it has not worked.

State verbs do not go continuous. Not I’ve been knowing him for years but I’ve known him for years. The same list as Unit 1 recycled: know, believe, own, understand, seem.

The mistake to avoid. A number of finished things takes the simple: not I’ve been reading three books this month but I’ve read three books this month.

The question form to learn. How long have you been working here? — almost always continuous, because how long asks about the activity itself.

Full grammar reference — present perfect simple vs present perfect continuous

What it is

Both forms connect the past to the present. The simple (have done) looks at the situation as a completed whole and draws attention to the result or the amount achieved. The continuous (have been doing) looks at the same stretch of time from the inside and draws attention to the activity and its duration.

What it means, and what it does

Scientists have explored several techniques reports what has been achieved: a finished set of results. Scientists have been exploring several techniques reports what they have been busy with: the work is ongoing, and it may not have produced anything yet. Both are true of the same research; they answer different questions — what have they got? versus what have they been doing?

When and why we use it

Both of these forms connect the past to the present, and both are perfect forms. The difference lies in the angle from which the speaker looks at the stretch of time. The simple looks at it from outside, as a completed whole, and draws attention to the result. The continuous looks at it from inside and draws attention to the activity and how long it has been going on.

Take a piece of research. Scientists have explored several techniques reports an achievement: this is what they now have. Scientists have been exploring several techniques reports an occupation: this is what they have been doing, and it may not have produced anything yet. Both sentences can be true of the same project; they answer different questions.

Two question words map onto the two forms almost perfectly and are the fastest practical guide. How long asks about duration and pulls the continuous. How many or how much asks about a completed quantity and pulls the simple. How long have you been reading it? versus How many pages have you read? Trying to count with the continuous — I’ve been writing three emails — is one of the clearest signals that the distinction has not been grasped.

The continuous also has a use that has nothing to do with duration: explaining something visible right now, even if the activity has just stopped. You’re out of breath — have you been running? And one restriction cuts across everything: state verbs have no continuous form at all, so with know, own, believe, belong the simple is your only option even when you mean duration.

Typical situations

You need this contrast for describing ongoing projects and research, explaining what you have been doing recently, talking about changes in the weather or the economy, and reporting progress at work.

  • A result you can see now — the simple, when the outcome is the point.Climate change has caused higher temperatures.
  • An activity that explains the present — the continuous, when the process is the point.Governments have been trying to reduce pollution.
  • How many, how much, how often — the simple, because you are counting a completed number.They’ve carried out six experiments this year.
  • How long — the continuous, because you are measuring a stretch of activity.They’ve been working on it for quite some time.
  • A completed action with a present consequence — the simple.One team has discovered a way to use lasers.
  • An unfinished or repeated activity — the continuous, often with recently, lately, all week.The seasonal rains have been arriving later and later.
  • A temporary situation up to now — the continuous.I’ve been staying with my sister while the roof is repaired.

How it differs from similar structures

How long…? → continuous (duration of activity) · How many / how much…? → simple (completed quantity). How long have you been reading it? vs How many pages have you read?
simple = finished, with a result · continuous = ongoing, possibly unfinished. I’ve painted the kitchen (it’s done) vs I’ve been painting the kitchen (that’s why I’m covered in paint).

How to build it

Present perfect simple: subject + have / has + past participle
Present perfect continuous: subject + have / has + been + verb-ing
Negative: haven’t / hasn’t (+ been) + …
Question: Have / Has + subject (+ been) + …?
Simple — affirmativeIt has caused floods. · We’ve done a lot.
Simple — negativeWe haven’t been very successful.
Simple — questionWhat have they found? · How many have they tested?
Continuous — affirmativeIt has been causing problems. · They’ve been working on it.
Continuous — negativeThey haven’t been working on it long.
Continuous — questionHow long has it been getting warmer?
Short answersYes, they have. / No, it hasn’t. — the same for both forms.
ContractionsI’ve been, she’s been, we’ve been — been is the marker of the continuous.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • The whole auxiliary chain is weak: have been reduces to /əv bɪn/ and has been to /əz bɪn/. In fast speech I’ve been working can sound like ‘I bin working’.
  • been is the one syllable that survives, so it is the cue to listen for when deciding which form you heard.
  • In short answers the auxiliary is stressed and never contracted: Yes, they have.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • State verbs do not take the continuous, so with know, believe, own, belong the simple is the only option even when you mean duration: I’ve known her for years, never I’ve been knowing.
  • With live, work, study, teach and other long-term activity verbs, both forms are used with for / since and the difference is very small: I’ve worked here for five years = I’ve been working here for five years.
  • The continuous often carries a hint that the activity is temporary or recent, while the simple sounds more permanent. He’s been living in Almaty suggests a stay; He’s lived in Almaty suggests a settled fact.
  • The continuous can explain a visible present state even if the activity has just stopped: You’re out of breath — have you been running?
  • Do not use the continuous to count: I’ve been writing three emails. Numbers and quantities belong with the simple.
  • Neither form works with a finished time expression: last week and in 2019 force the past simple, exactly as in Lesson 14.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I’ve been knowing him since 2015. → I’ve known him since 2015.Know is a state verb and has no continuous.
  • Scientists have been finding three new methods. → Scientists have found three new methods.A counted quantity takes the simple.
  • How long have you read that book? → How long have you been reading that book?How long about an activity takes the continuous.
  • They have been explored this for years. → They have been exploring this for years.The continuous needs been + -ing, not the participle.
  • It has been rain a lot lately. → It has been raining a lot lately.Been must be followed by the -ing form.
  • We’ve been trying to reduce pollution last year. → We tried to reduce pollution last year.A finished time forces the past simple.

More examples in context

  • resultClimate change has caused more storms, floods and droughts.
  • ongoing activityGovernments have been trying to reduce pollution for decades.
  • countingScientists have carried out dozens of experiments with cloud seeding.
  • durationNeil has been researching weather control for the last two years.
  • discoveryA team in Geneva has discovered a way of using lasers.
  • trendThe seasonal rains have been arriving later and later.
  • visible evidenceThe ground is soaked — it has been raining all night.
  • state verb, simple onlyWe’ve known about the greenhouse effect since the 1970s.
  • temporaryI’ve been staying with friends while the flat is repaired.
  • question pairHow long have you been working here? — How many projects have you finished?

A tip for remembering it

Ask which question your sentence is answering. How long? What have you been busy with? Why do you look like that? → continuous. How many? How much? What have you achieved? → simple. Then check for a state verb — if there is one, the simple is your only option.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Both link past to present: the simple shows a result, the continuous shows an activity.
  2. Continuous = have / has + been + -ing; the word been is the marker.
  3. How long? takes the continuous; how many / how much? takes the simple.
  4. State verbs (know, own, believe) have no continuous form.
  5. The continuous can explain something visible right now, even if the action has just stopped.
  6. A finished time expression rules out both and forces the past simple.
